questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -9 \\ 11\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y-(-9)}{2}=\frac{z-11}{0}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y+9}{2}=\frac{z-11}{0},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{z-11}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=11:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7-3t \\ -9+2t \\ 11\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-11}{0}$ part and instead write $z=11$, as follows:

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y+9}{2},\,z=11
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-4)}{0}=\frac{y-5}{3}=\frac{z-1}{2}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+4}{0}=\frac{y-5}{3}=\frac{z-1}{2},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+4}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-4:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5+3t \\ 1+2t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+4}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-4$, as follows:

$$
\frac{y-5}{3}=\frac{z-1}{2},\,x=-4
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
We have the vector equation 

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(2,-3,7)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨-5,2,-1⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{-5}=\frac{y-(-3)}{2}=\frac{z-7}{-1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{-5}=\frac{y+3}{2}=\frac{z-7}{-1}.
$$

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(-1,3,7)$ and $Q(3,-1,1).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨3,-1,1⟩-⟨-1,3,7⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-4,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-(-1)}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-4}=\frac{z-7}{-6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+1}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-4}=\frac{z-7}{-6}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14151155/assets/8722b93655e069e2f35147b572c16ed7af408a86f8a88597c79aea8fe59e9c4d.png)

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(2,-1,3)$ and $Q(4,-3,3).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨4,-3,3⟩-⟨2,-1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-3}{0}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-3}{0}.
$$

But the above equation is problematic because $\frac{z-3}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=3.$ For example, our two points $P(2,-1,3)$ and $Q(4,-3,3)$ both have $z$-coordinates of $z=3.$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-3}{0}$ part and instead write $z=3,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-2},\,z=3.
$$
